data.title: Malicious Root-Certificate Installation
data.summary: The sample installs an operator-controlled root or intermediate certificate into the system's trust store, allowing it to intercept TLS traffic or make its own malicious code appear validly signed.
data.description:
Once a certificate is trusted at the root or intermediate level, anything it signs — a
TLS connection it is interposed on, a binary it countersigns — is accepted as legitimate by
every application that relies on the system trust store, not only the sample itself. This
is a powerful, broad-reaching capability because it affects trust decisions made by
unrelated software on the host, well beyond whatever the sample directly does.
data.recommendation:
* Enumerate the certificate trust store for any root or intermediate certificate not matching a known-good baseline, rather than relying on signature validation that the rogue certificate would itself pass.
* Remove the rogue certificate and treat every TLS session and signed artefact validated against it during the exposure window as untrusted, pending independent verification.
* Audit for an associated interception proxy or configuration change (browser or system proxy settings) that the certificate was installed to support.
data.short_recommendation: Enumerate the trust store directly for rogue certificates; signature validation itself will not catch what the rogue certificate signs.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Added an operator-generated root certificate to the system trust store via the standard certificate-management API, then configured a local proxy to intercept TLS traffic using it.

mbc_techniques.implementation: Installed a rogue root certificate into the system trust store to support local TLS interception.
